Asymmetric sequential annulation/aldol process
of 4-isothiocyanato pyrazolones and allenones:
access to novel spiro[pyrrole–pyrazolones] and
spiro[thiopyranopyrrole–pyrazolones]†
Wenyao Wang, Xiaoze Bao, Shiqiang Wei, Shah Nawaz, Jingping Qu
 and
Baomin Wang
 *
A catalytic asymmetric sequential annulation/aldol reaction of
4-isothiocyanato pyrazolones and allenyl ketones has been developed,
which furnished a series of spiro[pyrrole–pyrazolone] heterocycles and
structurally novel spiro[thiopyranopyrrole–pyrazolone] derivatives in
good yields with high to excellent enantioselectivities. Notably, parallel
resolution of racemic spiro[pyrrole–pyrazolones] was achieved by a
catalyst-controlled asymmetric intramolecular vinylogous aldol pro-
cess. Structure diversity of the product was further enhanced by ready
transformations.
Nitrogen-containing five-membered heterocycles are ubiquitous
motifs found in various natural products, pharmaceutical
agents, agrochemicals and synthetic materials.
1 Accordingly,
the development of new eﬃcient methods toward their construc-
tion has long been a sought-after research topic in synthetic
organic chemistry.
2 Within this context, 2,3-allenyl carbonyl
compounds have emerged as a versatile class of building block
for the construction of chiral pyrrolidine derivatives.
3 In this
regard, seminal contributions from the Lu group are of par-
ticular note, who reported the [3+2] cyclization process between
2,3-allenoates and imines with phosphine catalysis, leading to
the formation of pyrroline rings with the allenoate being a three-
carbon component.
4 Later, the asymmetric version of this reac-
tion was extensively explored by using various chiral phosphine
or amine-based nucleophilic catalysts (Scheme 1a). 5 Other than
working as a three-carbon synthon, 2,3-allenyl carbonyl com-
pounds as a two-carbon partner were also engaged in the
asymmetric construction of pyrrolidine derivatives, as exemplified
by the chiral phosphoric acid c atalyzed [3+2] cycloaddition
between azomethine ylides and 2,3-allenoates pioneered by Gong
and co-workers (Scheme 1b).
6 However, compared to the well-
established Lu reaction, the synthetic potential of 2,3-allenyl

wondered whether 2,3-allenyl carbonyl compounds could be
engaged as a two-carbon component in an asymmetric annulation
with the 4-isothiocyanato pyrazolone synthon to forge a chiral spiro
2H-pyrrole scaﬀold (Scheme 1c). Herein, we report our successful
realization of this assumption.
We commenced our studies by surveying the reaction of
4-isothiocyanato pyrazolone1a and phenyl allenone 2a in the
presence of cinchona alkaloid catalysts (Table 1). An initial trial
revealed that the reaction could hardly stop at the product3aa,b u ti t
instead continued to add to another molecule of phenyl allenone2a
to give the product 4aa together with the intramolecular aldol
cyclization product5aa. In order to ensure the full conversion of
1a, in the following screening experiments 2.5 equivalent of 2a
was used.
Natural quinine ( Q1) was first examined as the catalyst, and
the reaction proceeded rapidly in dichloromethane (DCM) to
give the cascade spiroannulation/sulfa-Michael addition pro-
duct 4aa in 59% yield and 31% ee, along with the formation of
aldol cyclization product 5aa in 20% yield (entry 1). A similar
product distribution was observed when quinidine ( Q2) was
used but with decreased ee of 11% favoring the antipode of 4aa
(entry 2). Next, quinine-derived hydrogen bonding catalysts
were examined. While quinine thiourea Q3 aﬀorded 4aa in
59% yield and 52% ee (entry 3), to our delight, the use of
quinine squaramide catalyst Q4 improved the enantioselectivity
to 91% ee. Then, using Q4 as the optimal catalyst, a series of
solvents were screened (entries 5–9). The result indicated that
except for acetonitrile, other solvents including chloroform
(CHCl
3), tetrahydrofuran (THF) and 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE)
showed better enantioselectivities than DCM. Pleasingly, when
the reaction was run in toluene, the ee value could be increased
to 99% with a 66% yield of 4aa (entry 7). Given the extremely
high efficiency of Q4, reactions with lower catalyst loadings were
investigated. Thus, with 5 or 2.5 mol% Q4, still a very fast
reaction was observed, without any loss of the product yield
but with decreased ee values to 97% and 82%, respectively
(entries 10 and 11). Notably, without any catalyst, this reaction
also proceeded smoothly to completion within 6 h and 4aa was
formed in 80% yield in racemic form.
With the optimal conditions determined, we investigated
the generality of this new cascade reaction. A diverse array of
the 4-isothiocyanato pyrazolones was first surveyed. As demon-
strated in Scheme 2, pyrazolones with various substituents on
the phenyl ring at the C3 position of the pyrazolone framework,
as exemplified by methyl, fluorine, and methoxyl groups were
smoothly converted to the corresponding products in good
yields with excellent enantioselectivities of 93–99% ee (4ba–4da).
The polycyclic aromatic and heteroaromatic substituents at the C3
position of the pyrazolones were also compatible under standard
reaction conditions, generating the desired product 4ea, 4fa and
4ga in good yields with 79%, 99% and 77% ee, respectively. In
addition, the alkyl groups at the C3 position were also accom-
modated, as the methyl, ethyl, isopropyl and cyclopropyl substi-
tuted pyrazolones furnished the products4ha, 4ia, 4ja and 4ka in
40–81% yield with 89–97% ee.

Next, the substrate scope with respect to the allenyl ketone
partner was evaluated. To our delight, all tested 1-aryl allenic
ketones with electron-donating and electron-withdrawing
groups such as methyl, isopropyl, halogen and cyano groups
at the para-, meta-o r ortho-positions were well accommodated
in this process, aﬀording the corresponding products ( 4ab–4ag)
in good yields with excellent enantioselectivities (92–99% ee).
Notably, 1-naphthyl and 2-thienyl allenic ketones also generated
the desired products 4ah and 4ai in good yields with excellent
enantioselectivities of 89% ee and 95% ee. Besides, the aliphatic
allenyl ketone was well accommodated (4aj). The geometry of the
olefinic double bond of the side chain was determined to be Z by
NOE study of 4af (for details see the ESI †).
To evaluate the practical utility of the current catalytic system,
a scale-up reaction was performed with 4-isothiocyanato pyrazo-
lone 1a (2.5 mmol), phenyl allenone 2a (6.3 mmol), and Q4
(0.25 mmol), and the cascade spiroannulation/sulfa-Michael
addition was achieved smoothly to aﬀord 4aa in 66% yield with
97% ee on a gram-scale (Scheme 3). Further transformations of
the products were also conducted (see the ESI, † for details).
It is worth noting that the polyheterocyclic product 5aa
observed in the condition optimization stage is structurally
novel and interesting, which could actually be obtained in 68%
yield by prolonging the reaction time to 36 h and presumably
ought to be derived from compound 4aa through an intra-
molecular vinylogous aldol reaction. Given the marked struc-
tural novelty, as demonstrated by both spiro and fused ring
patterns featuring pyrazolone, 2H-pyrrole, and thiopyran frame-
works in 5aa, we set out to investigate the construction of
5 after the eﬀective synthetic protocol to 4 was established.
Hence, as summarized in Table 2, when DABCO or Et
3N was
used for 4af as a model substrate, the aldol cyclization product
5af and 50af could be obtained in good total yield but with low
dr (entries 1 and 2). We were pleased to find that Q4 furnished
improved activity and selectivity, and the corresponding
spiro[thiopyranopyrrole–pyrazolone] 5af was furnished in high
yield with excellent dr and ee values (entry 3). It turned out that
the diastereoselectivity of the reaction is controlled by the
chiral catalyst, and the spirostereocenter in 4af has no directing
effect, which was different from Evans aldol additions.
11 Then,
Q4 catalyzed asymmetric vinylogous aldol reaction of various 4
was investigated. As shown in Scheme 4, the yield and stereo-
selectivity could be sustained at a very high level for a wide
variety of pyrazolones substituted with different groups at the
C3 position, affording a series of chiral fused-thiopyran scaf-
folds, an important core of a large family of medicinally
relevant compounds.
12 Furthermore, the absolute configu-
ration of 5af was determined by X-ray crystallographic analysis.
Inspired by the success of the above catalyst-controlled
asymmetric aldol cyclization, t he parallel resolution of race-
mic compounds 4 to enantioenriched products 5 catalyzed by
cinchona alkaloids was next conducted (see Table S1 in the
ESI,† for details). To our delight, Q4 exhibited superior
reactivity and stereocontrol outcome aﬀording the aldol
product 5af within 12 h in a 45% yield with 99% ee, and
the product 5
00 af in 43% yield with 91% ee which is the
enantiomer of 50af, and the absolute configuration of 500 af
was determined by X-ray crystallographic analysis (see ESI, †
for details). And a series of diastereomer pairs of
spiro[thiopyranopyrrole–pyr azolones] under the optimal
reaction conditions were obta ined in good yield with excel-
lent enantioselectivity (Scheme 5).

In conclusion, we have developed an eﬃcient and facile
catalytic asymmetric [3+2] annulation of 4-isothiocyanato pyrazo-
lones and allenyl ketones. This r eaction aﬀorded spiro[pyrrole–
pyrazolone] products with excelle nt enantio-selectivities with a
broad substrate scope. And notably, a further catalyst-controlled
asymmetric vinylogous aldol cyclization delivered the spiro[thio-
pyranopyrrole–pyrazolone] derivatives readily in good yields with
excellent stereoselectivities. Rac emic spiro[pyrrole–pyrazolones]
could also be converted into enantioenriched spiro[thiopyrano-
pyrrole–pyrazolone] diastereomer pairs.
